title: Psychiatric advance directives
summary: A psychiatric advance directive (PAD) is a legal document in which a person, while well, records their preferences for mental health treatment during a future crisis, names someone to decide for them, or both. About half of US states have a specific PAD law; others use general health care directive laws, and the rules on when clinicians may override a PAD differ. Clinicians can help clients complete one and link it to relapse and safety plans. This page is information, not legal advice.
keyPoints: An instructional PAD records preferences, such as medicines that helped or did not, hospitals, people to contact, and care for children or pets. A proxy PAD names an agent to make decisions if the person loses capacity.
States differ on witnesses, how long a PAD lasts, whether it can be revoked during a crisis, and when providers may act against it, for example during involuntary treatment or an emergency.
Hospitals and other facilities in Medicare and Medicaid must tell adults about their right to make advance directives (42 CFR 489.102).
A facilitated conversation with a trained helper made people with serious mental illness more likely to complete a PAD in a randomized trial.
A PAD works best when copies are with the agent, the treatment team and the client, and when it is reviewed after each crisis.
whatToDo: Raise PADs when the client is well, for example while building a relapse prevention or safety plan.
Use your state's official form and instructions, and help the client think through preferences and an agent.
With the client's permission, share copies with their agent and treatment team, and note where the PAD is kept.
Review the PAD with the client after a crisis or a change in treatment.
Consult your licensing board or a healthcare attorney about your state's PAD law and when it can be overridden.
questions: Has the client had a chance to think about this while well, without pressure?
Who does the client trust to decide for them, and does that person agree?
Do the treatment team and crisis services know the PAD exists and how to find it?
